description: Hello! I’m Amjad from Morocco, passionate about AI, data, space, and solving real problems. I’m building a team for the Field Shift challenge to use NASA data to help Moroccan farmers improve crop rotation and water management. I’m seeking teammates in Python, data/AI, web development, UI/UX, agriculture, Earth science, or storytelling. Beginners are welcome!
summary: SeasonReplay is a free web app, in English and French, that helps rainfed farmers in Morocco’s Chaouia and Doukkala regions choose crop rotations that protect their soil and hold up in a hotter, drier climate. It compares four rotations, including today’s wheat after wheat, by replaying each one on the real 2011-2025 seasons measured by NASA POWER (daily rain, heat and root zone soil moisture), and shows the seasons that would have lost money, the profit, a climate score and the soil benefits of each. In Chaouia, wheat after wheat would have lost money in 9 of 15 seasons; barley then faba bean in only 1. Farmers set their own priorities and test what-if scenarios, see their land through MODIS and SMAP layers from NASA GIBS, learn when the sowing rains usually arrive from a Python model we tested honestly (the simple baseline beat machine learning), and get irrigation advice per crop from a Simulink model with a low-cost ESP32 soil sensor. This matters because Morocco’s seasons are already shifting while most farmers still plant as they did 30 years ago: SeasonReplay turns 35 years of NASA data into clear choices that protect both the soil and the farmer’s income, and says openly what the model does not know.
details:
SeasonReplay is a free web app, in English and French, that helps rainfed farmers in Morocco’s Chaouia (Settat) and Doukkala (Sidi Bennour) regions choose crop rotations that protect their soil and survive a changing climate.

NASA POWER daily data for 1991-2005 and 2011-2025 shows the shift. Hot spring days rose from 13.5 to 18.4 per year in Chaouia. Dry seasons went from 1 to 3 per 15 years in Chaouia and from 4 to 7 in Doukkala. Average rainfall barely moved, which is why farmers can miss the change.

  • Compare rotations (main feature): wheat after wheat (today’s practice), wheat → chickpea, barley → faba bean and wheat → lentil → barley are replayed on the real 2011-2025 seasons. A transparent model combines a water balance, heat stress at flowering and root zone soil moisture. For each rotation the app shows the seasons at a loss, the profit per hectare, the result in the driest year, the extra water needed, and the soil benefits (nitrogen, ground cover, organic matter, pest break, forage), with risks and what must be checked locally. In Chaouia, wheat after wheat would have lost money in 9 of 15 seasons, and barley → faba bean in 1. Farmers set their own priorities, and what-if sliders replay the seasons with less rain or more heat.
  • Planting time (Python): a logistic regression trained on 20 years of NASA data estimates when the autumn sowing rains arrive, using the INRA threshold of 25 mm in 10 days. On five unseen autumns the simple historical baseline scored better (Brier 0.253 vs 0.259 at Settat), so the app shows the baseline as the main indicator and says so. We cross-checked NASA rainfall against UCSB CHIRPS.
  • See it from space: MODIS vegetation and SMAP soil moisture layers from NASA GIBS on an Esri ArcGIS map, comparing the wet spring of 2018 with the dry spring of 2023.
  • Smart irrigation (MATLAB/Simulink): an FAO-56 root zone water balance with ESP32 sensor noise and an on/off valve. The app runs it in the browser for every crop, using its own crop coefficient and root depth.
  • Field sensor: a low-cost ESP32 soil probe (about 150 MAD) compares the farmer’s plot with the satellite estimate. A 3D concept of the solar field unit was made in SolidWorks.
  • Also included: crop ranking, an income simulator, a season calendar and a plain-language guide.

Benefits
Fewer failed harvests, less wasted water, better decisions before buying seed and fertilizer, and healthier soil thanks to legumes that fix nitrogen. The app is free, and the sensor is cheap enough for small farms.

Intended impact
We want to give smallholders and extension agents a way to test a change on 15 real seasons before risking a harvest. The next steps are to validate the crop parameters with INRA Morocco and with farmers, add a Darija interface and SMS alerts, and field-test the sensor.

Tools

  • Data: NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS (MODIS, SMAP), UCSB CHIRPS.
  • Code: JavaScript and Node.js data pipeline; Python (NumPy, logistic regression); React, Vite, Recharts, Esri ArcGIS Maps SDK, hosted on Vercel.
  • Engineering: MATLAB/Simulink, SolidWorks, ESP32/Arduino.
  • Collaboration: GitHub.

How it is creative
Instead of predicting the future, SeasonReplay replays the past: every rotation is tested on seasons that really happened, so farmers can trust the result. It connects three scales: the region from space, 35 years of climate, and a single plot through the sensor. It is also honest about its limits: the ML result that lost to the baseline is shown openly, and every assumption is listed.

Factors we considered

  • Farmers’ real constraints: seed and buyer access, labour, livestock, water.
  • Soil health alongside income.
  • Satellite resolution against field reality.
  • Uncertainty in crop prices and yields, labelled as provisional.
  • Language and simplicity for non-expert users.
  • That the tool supports the farmer’s judgment and never replaces it.
